\section{Three Scenarios for the Lending Environment}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Prose budget 1,150 words (SOL_PLAN_REFORMAT.md). Every number is read from
% thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex, tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, generated by
% notebooks/scripts/build_results_tables.py from results/raw; nothing is typed.

\label{sec:levers}
We address RQ3 through three scenarios. Each regulatory switch is compared with the benchmark, both with and without peer influence:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Bureau visibility} ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{bur}}$): \ac{BNPL} obligations reach the bureau and enter the Regulation 23A test, closing the asymmetry of Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}; the model's representation of the 2026 reporting requirement \cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}, subject to the limit stated there.
\item \textbf{Mandatory affordability screening} ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{aff}}$): the Regulation 23A test is applied to \ac{BNPL} originations themselves, the South African analogue of the \ac{FCA}'s proportionate affordability check \cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}.
\item \textbf{Peer effects} ($\beta > 0$): adoption is socially transmitted through Equation~\ref{eq:peer}. A behavioural mechanism rather than an instrument, it is a scenario because it asks whether the answers to the other two depend on how adoption spreads; its $\beta = 0$ arm is the control of every comparison.
\end{enumerate}
The experimental grid crosses the benchmark, bureau visibility and mandatory screening with $\beta=0$ and $\beta=1$.
This separates each regulatory effect from its interaction with peer adoption.
The reported \ac{NCR} position on incidental credit is relevant to the late fees in Submodel~14 (Section~\ref{sec:background}).
The baseline retains a light origination screen as a modelling assumption; Scenario~2 tests mandatory affordability assessment without assuming that incidental-credit classification alone settles which provisions apply.
We compare cumulative \ac{BNPL} volume as well as default to distinguish borrowing deferred within the horizon from borrowing not undertaken during it.
Table~\ref{tab:scenarios} reports the same panel of outcomes in every cell, and Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios} plots its default and volume rows.

Bureau visibility, the 2026 reporting requirement represented through its affordability channel only, does not lower default in that channel: it raises the rate by $0.26 \pm 0.11$ points without peer influence and changes it by $0.04 \pm 0.12$ points with it, while the scoring channel remains outside the model.
The first result has a mechanism.
Once \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the Regulation 23A test, the traditional lender refuses more applications, 1{,}160 against 1{,}033 in the benchmark.
The refusals fall on households that already carry \ac{BNPL} instalments and now ask for traditional credit to cover a shortfall; the visible obligation makes the gate stricter without making the household more solvent, and a refused household is left with its gap.
The 90+ day arrears share among credit-active households is unchanged ($-0.06 \pm 0.13$ points), so the addition is at the margin of population default rather than in the depth of arrears.
Cumulative \ac{BNPL} volume moves by less than 1\% in either arm, so visibility neither defers nor deters \ac{BNPL} borrowing: the instrument acts on the traditional lender's decision and leaves the \ac{BNPL} agreement untouched.

Mandatory screening applies the same test to \ac{BNPL} originations.
It refuses more \ac{BNPL} requests than the benchmark's light screen, which shows in adoption (15.10\% against 16.71\% at the final tick without peer influence, 62.97\% against 65.56\% with it) and in volume, which falls by 1.8\% and 1.6\%.
Default does not move: $+0.02 \pm 0.10$ and $-0.05 \pm 0.10$ points.
The requests the test screens out are a small share of a volume that is already sized to each household's discretionary budget, and the households it protects are not those that default: default in the model follows from an income shock that outlasts the buffer, which no origination screen observes in advance.

On the defer-versus-desist criterion, both instruments leave cumulative volume within 2\% of the benchmark.
Neither defers borrowing within the horizon nor deters it, because the volume households take on is set by their demand for purchases and the per-platform limits, and neither instrument reaches either.
Peer influence changes the level and not the ranking: at $\beta = 1$ default is between 0.6 and 0.8 points higher in every cell than at $\beta = 0$, adoption is four times higher and cumulative volume twelve times higher, yet the differences between scenarios within a row are the same nulls.
Socially transmitted adoption creates no policy interaction; neither instrument works better, or worse, in a market where \ac{BNPL} spreads through peers.

Section~\ref{sec:results-stacking} explains why.
Platforms that cannot see one another produce stacking: with four platforms 45\% of households holding \ac{BNPL} carry two or more facilities, and none can with one.
Yet default is the same with one platform as with six.
The harm comes from the additional obligations \ac{BNPL} creates, not from their being spread across firms.
Both instruments act on a single agreement, one by making it visible to the traditional lender and the other by screening it, and neither changes how much a household takes on, so neither moves default.
The only lever in the model that does is a cap on the agreements a household may hold open at once (Appendix~\ref{app:levers}), which acts on the number of concurrent obligations and which no jurisdiction imposes; the cooling-off window, reported there too, cuts volume where adoption is social and lowers default by no more than $0.55 \pm 0.12$ points.

RQ3 is therefore answered: neither instrument changes distress in the affordability channel, with or without peer adoption.
The reporting requirement's scoring channel, by which reported \ac{BNPL} behaviour lowers scores and raises the price or refusal of credit, is outside the model and may do what the affordability channel does not; the result bounds only the channel modelled (Section~\ref{sec:lim-reading}).
The policy direction that follows concerns mechanism, not a statutory threshold: an instrument that would move default in this model must limit the number of agreements a household services at once, and neither reporting nor screening does.
